final_message:
All five versions are written and built, and each one prints the exact expected output for all three samples. Each also matches an independent Python reference on 10 generated edge-case files and on a 2M-line benchmark-sized file.

**Algorithm (same in all five):** read the whole file, then one pass over the bytes. Each line is checked against the SPEC regex by hand-written byte matching, with no regex engine. The path template is built into a reusable buffer and looked up in a hash table, and each latency is stored as tenths in an integer array. At the end each template's latencies are sorted, p50/p95/max are picked by nearest rank, and the top 10 are chosen by count then name.

**Choices for speed:**
- **C++:** memchr for newlines, `std::unordered_map` with transparent lookup so a line never allocates, `std::sort`, `std::partial_sort` for the top 10. `_setmode` keeps the output LF. This needs the MSVC CRT, not just the standard library.
- **Java:** byte-array parsing into static fields so a line allocates nothing; `HashMap` keyed by the template string; `long[]` per template; `Arrays.sort`. Output uses `\n` explicitly because `println` would emit CRLF.
- **C#:** pointer parsing (the csproj already allows unsafe), vectorized `IndexOf` for newlines, `Array.Sort` on `long[]`, and raw byte output. I turned off tiered compilation and background GC in `solution.csproj` (no package references added), which took the run from about 1.6 s to about 1.0 s.
- **Go:** `bytes.IndexByte`, `m[string(bytes)]` lookups that don't allocate, generic `slices.Sort`.
- **JS:** `Buffer.indexOf` for newlines; a custom FNV hash table over template bytes (no string per line); `Float64Array` latencies sorted natively.

**Big-latency handling:** latencies too large for a 64-bit integer (possible under the regex, e.g. 25-digit integer parts) go into a rare string path that sorts by length then bytes and prints exactly. The fast-path limit is 19 digits in C++ and Go, 18 in Java and C# (signed `long`), and 15 in JS (exact doubles).

**Samples:** C++, Java, C#, Go and JS each pass s1, s2 and s3, plus 10 generated edge-case files. Those files cover leading zeros, 15–25-digit latencies, odd status classes, empty and digit-only segments, quotes in queries and user agents, and malformed variants.

**Timings** (one run of each on the 2M-line, ~181 MB generated file, rough and single-machine):
- C++: about 0.85–1.0 s
- Go: about 1.1–1.4 s
- C#: about 1.0 s after the csproj change
- Java: about 1.7–1.8 s, run directly
- JS: about 2.1 s

I did not profile further, so the C++ gap to Go and C# is unexplained.

**Things to know:**
- The build environment's PATH is about 8,100 characters. `vcvars64.bat` pushes it past cmd's limit, so `cpp\build.cmd` failed until I built with a minimal PATH. The benchmark machine presumably has a shorter PATH, but check this.
- The benchmark generator I wrote uses about 300 path shapes, which is my guess at the real data. The sample s3 has 222 templates, so it looks similar.
- Helper scripts are in `tools/`: `ref.py` (reference), `gen.py` (generator), `check.sh` (runs a program against all test files), `java_wrap.sh`. I deleted the scratch folder with the large bench input.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
